summary: Cape Mendocino Light, first lit in 1868 on California's westernmost headland, was moved to Shelter Cove in 1998 and is now a museum.

structures.note: 43-foot (13 m) iron tower, moved 1998-99 to Shelter Cove

access.note: Museum at Shelter Cove run by a volunteer society; open most months, with docents in summer.

facts.agency: Cape Mendocino Lighthouse Preservation Society (per LighthouseFriends); the society's site says Humboldt County owns the building

events.note: Lighthouse Board notice: tower recently erected on the western slope of the cape
March 1871 earthquake made the brick keepers' duplex uninhabitable
Boat from tender Manzanita capsized in surf; three men drowned, including Inspector Charles J. McDougal
Blunts Reef lightship stationed off the cape (LighthouseFriends); on the coast in 1915 as Light Vessel No. 83
1906 earthquake destroyed the wooden oil house
22 January 1923 earthquake: assistant keeper's quarters and oil house cracked; second shock 27 January
Keeper Palmer raised the alarm for the burning steam schooner Everett; crew saved (LighthouseFriends)
Coast Guard took control of the station
Fresnel lens installed in a replica tower at the Humboldt County Fairgrounds, Ferndale
Light moved from the tower lantern to a nearby pole; last head keeper transferred
Blunts Reef lightship withdrawn and replaced by a large navigational buoy
Tower lantern lifted off by helicopter in November 1998 and moved to Shelter Cove
Society site says opened May 2000; LighthouseFriends gives dedication September 2000 and public opening Memorial Day 2001
Modern light on the cape discontinued and removed, 29 May 2013

corrections.why: The record point is the tower after its 1998 move to Shelter Cove. The station's original site on the cape is given by the USLHS place record as 40.43717, -124.40283. A human should decide whether the map shows the original station, the relocated tower, or both.

corrections.proposed: 1951 light moved from the tower lantern to a nearby pole; no second tower
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes a 1951 move of the light from the tower to a pole and no second tower. No source found for a 'Tower 2'.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources give 1951 and 2013. LighthouseFriends says the light was moved from the tower lantern to a pole in 1951, and the modern light on the cape was discontinued in 2013.
The record's point is the relocated tower at Shelter Cove. The original station on the cape is about 500 m or more away, as the USLHS place record and the Preservation Society's history place it.

notes_for_editor: Construction-era sources: the Light-House Board volumes before 1891 are not in the corpus. The 1868 first-light date rests on the New York Herald notice (source 2). The 1867 Shubrick loss, the 1868-71 construction and keeper facts, the 1881 drowning, the 1906 earthquake, the 1916 Bear and the 1926 Everett rescue, the 1939-2013 events and the 1998-2001 move rest on LighthouseFriends alone (source 1); each is marked as such in the story. The record's characteristic (Fl W 15s) is not sourced here: the 1868 notice gives a revolving white light with a five-second flash, and LighthouseFriends says one white flash every thirty seconds. The record's 'tower 2' (1951) and its 500 m position conflict are handled in corrections. Dates: the 1893 and 1895 Light-House Board reports are cited by scan page, since the printed page numbers were not confirmed. The 1893 chimney passage is OCR-garbled ('torn <lown'), so the quote is cut to 'The chimneys on the south side were torn'. The Tricolor wreck's date is the newspaper's date (28 July 1905); no primary gives the date of the wreck itself. Opening date: the society says May 2000; LighthouseFriends says Memorial Day 2001; both are kept in the story. The park is 'Mal Coombs Park' on the society's site and in the record but 'Mel Coombs Park' on LighthouseFriends. Ownership of the building is disputed (county per society; the society per LighthouseFriends). The USLHS place record says 'open_to_public: false', which conflicts with the society's summer opening. Keepers: 83 roster lines from the USLHS archive (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory), printed exactly and normalized by roster.py; the 'other' line (Coast Guard personnel, 1950 onward) is kept only in the roster. Mrs. G. A. May is listed as a first assistant. LighthouseFriends names her as May's wife. Adeline Corbett, Amelia Chism and Mary Marble are named in the story as the women in assistant posts. No keeper was found with a source connecting him to another station. Height disagreement (added in this check): the 1868 Herald notice gives the light 380 ft above mean sea level (source 2); LighthouseFriends gives 422 ft above the sea and the USLHS record 422 ft above mean high water (sources 1, 11). The story states both; facts.focal_height_m keeps 129 m from the 422 ft figure, which LighthouseFriends does not call focal height. Tricolor (1905): the lightship crew's dispute about the whistle and Wold's later admission of blame are now in the story (source 8). Bear wreck: the Commissioner's FY1916 report (source 13, scan p.190, printed page not confirmed) gives 15 June 1916; the wreck date in wrecks[] is now that date. LSB 1923: the 'damaged to some extent' and 'foundation being cracked' quotes are on PDF p.14 (source 6), not p.15; the 27 January shock is on p.15 (source 7). Lightship 1905 is not attributed to the Board in any source read; the story says 'a lightship was stationed'. Edward E. Charron (roster line 'other', from 1950, end not stated) is not named in the story; the roster line stays as the USLHS prints it. The 4:30 a.m. whistle time in the Tricolor story is the OCR reading '4:SO a- m.' taken as 4:30; the story repeats it.
